title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
claim: Samplers that keep a small, stable candidate pool as temperature rises preserve quality, while those admitting many low-probability tokens collapse.
layout: 2 panels, left illustrative bars with dot columns, right grouped bar chart
description: Two panels. Panel (a) shows a Llama-3.1-8B story excerpt in a rounded box, with three blue-highlighted candidate words (with, carrying, when). Below are two horizontal bar charts of the ten likeliest next tokens, one at Temperature 1 and one at Temperature 2. Beside each chart are columns of filled or hollow dots for top-nσ (blue), min-p (green) and top-p (orange), showing which tokens each rule keeps. A 'kept' row gives totals: 3/4/4 at T=1, and 3/8/51,845 at T=2. Panel (b) is a grouped bar chart of Qwen3.5 SWE-bench Verified issues resolved at temperature 2 across model sizes. Top-nσ in blue reaches 46–62 while top-p, top-k and Top-H sit at 0. The eye goes first to the blue bars and the large orange 51,845.
caption: (a) Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct partway through a science-fiction story (the step is picked by a fixed rule, Appendix [ref]). The box shows the text so far, with the three continuations top-$n\sigma$ keeps highlighted. The bars are the model's ten likeliest next tokens, each dot column marks the tokens one rule keeps, and the number under a column is that rule's total. Going from temperature 1 to 2 flattens the bars. Top-$n\sigma$ still keeps the same three words and min-$p$ only grows from 4 to 8, but top-$p$ 0.9 now needs 51,845 tokens, most of the 128K vocabulary, to reach 90% of the probability. (b) At temperature 2, Qwen3.5 agents using top-$p$, top-$k$ or Top-H resolve no SWE-bench Verified issues, while top-$n\sigma$ agents resolve 46--62% (100 issues per group, dashes mark samplers that were not run on the fresh issue sets).
abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.
